paras: The killing of Jake Marshall, his brother and Louis Payton took place at Jeanerette, Louisiana, on or shortly before February 7, 1888, when 'unknown persons' shot the three men after Marshall, a Black deputy sheriff, had killed a man named George Dixon. Marshall's brother and Payton, a spectator, died almost at once, and Marshall's body was later found in a swamp ditch. A single special dispatch to the New Orleans Picayune carried the story to papers across the country under headlines counting 'four men' dead.

According to the Picayune's Jeanerette correspondent, George Dixon was shot and killed by Jake Marshall, described as 'colored, a deputy sheriff,' in what the dispatch called an 'altercation' or, in other printings, a 'quarrel.' The dispatch gives no cause for the dispute and does not state Dixon's race.

After the shooting Marshall fled and hid in a corn crib, where he was found together with his brother. The two were fired upon, and the brother and Louis Payton were 'almost instantly killed.' Payton was a spectator who, in the Tribune's and the Sun's texts, had been 'warned to retire for fear of being shot.'

Marshall got away from the crib, but he had been hit, and his dead body was afterward discovered in a ditch in the swamps. The dispatch closed with the statement that 'the shooting was done by unknown persons,' and it named none of them.
No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution of the shooters appears in the coverage, and no follow-up from Louisiana was found.

The story reached readers almost entirely as one wire text, printed on February 8 in New York, St. Paul, Omaha, Indianapolis, Wichita and Waterbury. Headline writers treated it as a gunfight or brawl rather than mob violence: 'Four Men Killed in a Quarrel' in the New-York Tribune, 'Lively Times with Firearms' in the Sun, 'Shot by Unknown' in the St. Paul Globe, and 'Shooting for Blood' in the Wichita Eagle. The Omaha Bee counted 'Three Men Killed and One Fatally Wounded,' and the Maysville Evening Bulletin, a day later, 'Four Men Shot to Death in Louisiana.'

Weekly papers in Kentucky, Maryland, New Jersey, South Dakota and Kansas cut the item down over the following week, the Semi-Weekly Interior Journal to a single line that 'four persons were killed.' Every version identified Marshall as 'colored' while leaving the shooters unnamed, and none used the words 'mob' or 'lynching.'

The Maysville Bulletin datelined the item February 9, as it did every other wire story on the same page, while the papers that printed it a day earlier carried a February 7 dateline. The Democratic Messenger of Snow Hill, Maryland, condensed the dispatch to say that Marshall and his brother 'were overtaken and killed,' dropping his escape from the crib that the fuller texts describe. Accounts of his wounds also varied, from 'two wounds in his left arm' in the Tribune to 'fatal wounds' in the Globe.

reader.title: Killing of Jake Marshall, his brother and Louis Payton
bases: After Jake Marshall, a Black deputy sheriff, shot George Dixon, he was found hiding in a corn crib and he, his brother and a spectator were shot dead by 'unknown persons' (A1, A2, A3).

Three men were shot dead by 'unknown persons' who tracked Marshall to his hiding place after he killed Dixon, with no officer or arrest mentioned (A1, A2, A3); the papers give neither the number of shooters nor their motive, and none uses the words mob or lynching.
Every account is a copy or condensation of one special to the New Orleans Picayune from Jeanerette (A1, A3, A6); no local, follow-up or independent report was found.

accounts.label: Picayune special from Jeanerette (wire)
accounts.gist: Marshall killed Dixon in a quarrel, fled to a corn crib, and was found there with his brother; 'unknown persons' fired on them, killing the brother and the spectator Payton, and Marshall, though he escaped, was later found dead in a swamp ditch.

accounts.label: Condensed rewrite (Democratic Messenger)
accounts.gist: Marshall and his brother 'were overtaken and killed', as was Payton; no mention of the corn crib, the escape or the unknown shooters.

framing.detail: Papers ran the Picayune special nearly word for word under headlines of a quarrel or gunfight ('Four Men Killed in a Quarrel', 'Lively Times with Firearms', 'Shot by Unknown'), naming Marshall 'colored' and leaving the shooters unidentified.
Weekly digests cut the story to a few lines, one to a single sentence that 'four persons were killed'.

conflicts.note: The Feb. 9 dateline in the Maysville Bulletin, printed a day after the story appeared elsewhere, matches every other wire item on its page and is likely the paper's own redating; Feb. 7 is the better evidence.
